title: Factorial recursion and return value propagation
concept: The return value of a recursive function is passed in reverse order through the call stack.

steps.title: Include header files
steps.explanation:
Include the standard input/output library with **`#include <stdio.h>`** for use with `printf`.

In this lesson, we learn the second key to recursion --- **return value propagation**.

steps.title: Start main function - call factorial(4)
steps.explanation: **`int result = factorial(4);`** --- Although declaring `result`, calling `factorial(4)`, and storing the return value are all on one line, `result` is actually not populated until `factorial(4)` ends.

steps.title: Call factorial(4) -> factorial(3) -> factorial(2)
steps.explanation: **`return n * factorial(n - 1);`** --- We are trying to calculate `return 4 * factorial(3)` from factorial(4), but we do not know the result of factorial(3) yet. factorial(3) also tries to calculate `return 3 * factorial(2)`

steps.title: factorial(1) - Terminating condition (base case) reached!
steps.explanation: When we call factorial(1) from factorial(2), `n <= 1` is **true** --- we have finally reached the **termination condition**! It returns the value `1` immediately, without any further calls to itself.

steps.title: Return value propagation: 1 -> 2 -> 6
steps.explanation: Return values ​​are propagated in reverse order --- the most beautiful part of recursion. If factorial(1) returns **1**, factorial(2) returns `2 * 1 = 2`, factorial(3) returns `3 * 2 = 6`, and the frames are popped one by one.

steps.title: Final return: factorial(4) = 24
steps.explanation:
factorial(4) returns **24** with `return 4 * 6`, and the value is stored in `result` of main.

Recursion can usually be understood as two stages: a downward stage where the problem is broken down (winding), and an upward stage where the value obtained from the termination condition is taken up and synthesized (unwining).

steps.title: Result output
steps.explanation:
**`printf("4! = %d\n", result);`** --- Prints `24` in `result` as `%d` and displays `4!' on the screen.

To summarize the process of recursion passing the return value: When entering, break the big problem into smaller and smaller pieces (4!->3!->2!->1!), and when exiting, combine the smaller answers to create a larger answer.

quiz.question: When calling factorial(5), how many total times is the factorial function called?
quiz.explanation:
It is called a total of 5 times: factorial(5) -> factorial(4) -> factorial(3) -> factorial(2) -> factorial(1).
A termination condition has been reached in factorial(1) and no further calls will be made.

misconceptions.correct: It postpones the computation until the termination condition is reached and combines the results as it returns.
misconceptions.why: Since factorial(4) can be calculated only after knowing the result of factorial(3), the results are propagated in reverse order after all calls.

misconceptions.wrong: Recursion is always slower than loops
misconceptions.correct: Simple recursion has function call overhead, but when tail recursion optimization is applied, it has the same performance as a loop.
misconceptions.why: If the compiler detects tail recursion, it can convert it to a loop. However, this factorial is of the form n*factorial(n-1), so it is not tail recursive.

keyTakeaway: The return value of recursion is passed in reverse order up the call stack, starting from the termination condition.
